extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and others interested in United States patent litigation and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for judicial claim construction in U.S. patent infringement litigation (Markman hearings), including what evidence may be used, timing of hearings, and appellate review standards. Focused on how courts determine the meaning and scope of patent claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation is a matter of law (judge, not jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., the Supreme Court held that claim interpretation is a matter of law rather than a question of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat patents like contracts and therefore are best suited to interpret patent language; judges perform claim construction in a Markman hearing which usually defines the scope of the patent either for or against the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence — defined components
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence includes (1) the patent itself, (2) the patent specification, and (3) patent history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words themselves are the most important source of evidence; the court must analyze the words in their ordinary meaning and 'in light of the specifics . . . [of] the invention.' Patent specification and prosecution history are examined alongside the patent to determine intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the claim language (ordinary meaning in light of the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must analyze the claim language's plain or ordinary meaning and interpret it 'in light of the specifics . . . [of] the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words themselves are the most important source of evidence when defining the scope of the patent; courts start with the language of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as the 'dictionary' of the patent (35 U.S.C. §112 reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification contains 'a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it' per 35 U.S.C. §112 and is known as the dictionary of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must be consulted to determine whether the patentee used terms inconsistently with ordinary patent language; it must be read with the patent to understand meaning and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history informs claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent history (prosecution history) provides information regarding proceedings prior to patent approval, including applicant representations to the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history may provide the court with a more in-depth understanding as to the intended scope of the claim and is part of intrinsic evidence considered during claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence — definition and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence can include sources such as expert testimony and other external materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit case law debates extent of extrinsic evidence use; extrinsic evidence is generally auxiliary and may be used for background or to resolve ambiguity when intrinsic evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on extrinsic evidence (Vitronics → Pitney-Bowes → Teva rule evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vitronics stated extrinsic evidence should not be used when intrinsic evidence is sufficient; Pitney-Bowes allowed judges to consult extrinsic evidence even where intrinsic evidence was adequate; the Supreme Court in Teva (2015) clarified the modern approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current guiding rule (post-Teva): only intrinsic evidence should be used initially; if after intrinsic review the claim terms are still ambiguous, extrinsic evidence can be consulted. If there is a dispute over underlying facts, courts may make secondary factual findings about extrinsic evidence credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate standard of review for claim construction (de novo to hybrid clear-error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit originally applied de novo review to claim construction (Cybor en banc), meaning appellate courts reviewed without regard to the lower court's decision; Teva modified this, requiring deference to a trial court's factual findings absent clear error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Teva, appellate courts review legal conclusions de novo but must defer to the lower court's factual findings regarding extrinsic evidence unless clearly erroneous (hybrid standard). This change affected reversal rates and uniformity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of a Markman hearing — court discretion and possible stages
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Markman hearing occurs is up to the trial court; possible times include during pre-discovery, at summary judgment, and at trial but before jury instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has not mandated timing; courts choose based on case circumstances and implied preferences. Timing choice has trade-offs summarized below in pros/cons entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and disadvantages of conducting Markman early (pre-discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting a Markman hearing during the pre-discovery phase can limit litigation time and centralize discovery around the court's interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: limiting litigation time, early settlements, decreasing litigation costs, centralizing discovery. Disadvantages: short discovery phases, court interpreting claim language with little information, early constructions may later change making early hearings impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and disadvantages of conducting Markman at summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Most courts conduct Markman hearings at summary judgment prior to trial, using discovery to aid interpretation but risking appellate reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: identifying which claims are important and allowing discovery to inform claim construction. Disadvantages: higher likelihood of reversal on appeal (especially under prior de novo review), and before Teva appeals of factual findings may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and disadvantages of conducting Markman at or after trial (prior to jury instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding claim construction at or after trial (but before jury instructions) allows courts to consider all evidence and better understand the technology, but has other costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: judges have better understanding of the technology and have heard all important evidence. Disadvantages: delays in jury decisions, juries may hear evidence without official claim construction, and potential for unnecessary litigation over differing interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impacts of splitting claim construction from trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A major consequence of Markman hearings is the split of patent claims into a separate claim-construction hearing and a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include production of experts on two occasions, increased litigation costs, depletion of judicial resources, potential lengthening of litigation, and increased likelihood of reversal on appeal if claim construction is done without sufficient background information.
